item.title: Deep Sequence Model Reveals Disrupted Emotion‑Action Coupling in Adolescents with NSSI
item.description:
Deep Sequence Model Reveals Disrupted Emotion‑Action Coupling in Adolescents with NSSI

A new AI study submitted on 8 Oct 2026 combines an experimental pain paradigm, EEG microstate analysis, and an interpretable deep sequence model to uncover neurodynamic mechanisms linking social distress to non‑suicidal self‑injury (NSSI) in depressed adolescents.

🔍 Overview

  • Study population: 106 adolescents with depression (67 with NSSI, labeled DN+; 39 without NSSI, labeled DN-).
  • Conditions examined: social pain, physical pain, and resting‑state.
  • Goal: Identify brain‑state dynamics that differentiate DN+ from DN- during social pain.

🧩 How it works

  • Data acquisition: High‑density EEG recorded while participants experienced social and physical pain stimuli.
  • Microstate analysis: EEG segmented into recurring topographic patterns (microstates) labeled MS3, MS5, etc.
  • Deep sequence model: Integrated disease‑specific, domain‑adversarial, consistency, and contrastive learning objectives to capture higher‑order dependencies in microstate sequences.

⚙️ Key details

  • Classification performance: Social‑pain condition achieved 68.55% accuracy in distinguishing DN+ from DN-, an 8.94‑point improvement over the best baseline.
  • Neurodynamic findings:
    • DN+ adolescents showed weakened bidirectional transitions between MS3 and MS5 during social pain.
    • Source reconstruction linked MS3 to emotional/interoceptive processing and MS5 to action preparation, indicating disrupted emotion‑action coupling.
    • Time‑resolved analysis revealed:
      • Greater early‑to‑middle recruitment of action‑related states.
      • Later recruitment of emotion‑related states in DN+ participants.
  • Mediation patterns:
    • In DN- adolescents, MS5‑to‑MS3 dynamics mediated the link between social‑evaluation sensitivity and affective outcomes.
    • This mediation was absent in DN+ adolescents, while MS3‑to‑MS5 transitions correlated with increased negative affect in DN+.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a mechanistically interpretable neural signature for objective identification of NSSI.
  • Highlights disrupted emotion‑action coupling as a core neurodynamic mechanism in adolescents experiencing social pain.
  • Demonstrates the utility of interpretable deep sequence modeling for uncovering higher‑order brain‑state dependencies in clinical neuroscience.

#NSSI #EEG #DeepLearning #Neuroscience #AI

Source: Social Pain Disrupts Emotion-Action Brain-State Dynamics in Adolescents with Non-Suicidal Self-Injury

item.title: AI Is Cognitive Junk Food For Your Brain, Researchers Warn
item.description:
AI Is Cognitive Junk Food For Your Brain, Researchers Warn

A new analysis argues that artificial intelligence functions as a cognitive version of a hot dog, appealing in the moment but ultimately bad for cognitive health. The warning is grounded in neuroscience and evolutionary history, challenging the prevalent idea that the human brain is simply a biological computer.

🧩 Overview

The argument begins with a fundamental critique of how the AI industry views the human mind. The evidence suggests that while influential figures like Alan Turing, Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk have promoted the idea that the brain is a computer, this model is dangerously incomplete.

The evidence quotes a central claim: “AI, it turns out, is something like a cognitive version of a hot dog: It appeals to us in the moment, but undermines the health and sustainability of cognitive systems we’ve evolved over several millennia.”

🔍 How It Works

The problematic “brain as computer” model posits thought as a three-step algorithm:

  1. Input: The mind takes in information from the world.
  2. Computation: It manipulates that information.
  3. Output: It enacts behavior.

While this model has been productive in many ways, critics—including John von Neumann—doubted it could capture the “exceptional complexity of the human nervous system.”

An alternative model, championed by researcher Cisek, suggests that brains are better understood as feedback-control systems, not information processors. This is not a new idea: philosopher John Dewey described the mind as a circuit where “the motor response determines the stimulus, just as truly as sensory stimulus determines movement.”

Model Core Idea Proponents / Critics
Brain as computer Input, computation, output algorithm Alan Turing, Demis Hassabis, Elon Musk
Brain as feedback-control system Minds take action to adjust the stimulus they receive Cisek, John Dewey

A classic example from baseball illustrates the difference. To catch a fly ball, the feedback-control approach suggests a simple heuristic: “keep the ball in the same position within your visual field, and then move to maintain that situation.”

💡 Why It Matters

The evolutionary history of the nervous system supports the feedback-control view. The evidence states: “From ancient fish to amphibians to mammals to primates and eventually modern humans, what we observe is that new behaviors emerge in response to new environmental possibilities.” The nervous system’s history is described as one of “continuous extension of control further and further into the world.”

Norbert Wiener, godfather of cybernetics, is quoted: “The thought of every age is reflected in its technique.” The warning is that the current age’s technique—AI—may be reducing the cognitive complexity humans have evolved over millennia. As the evidence puts it, “humans are more complex than a straightforward comparison to computers gives us credit for — and far more than most of the AI industry seems to appreciate.”

#AIandCognition #Neuroscience #BrainAsComputer #FeedbackControl #CognitiveHealth #AIWarning

Source: Our minds aren’t equipped to handle AI

item.title: NS-Copilot: LLM‑Driven Multi‑Agent System for End‑to‑End Neuroscience Analysis
item.description:
NS-Copilot: LLM‑Driven Multi‑Agent System for End‑to‑End Neuroscience Analysis

A new system called NS‑Copilot has been introduced that uses large language models and a multi‑agent architecture to automate neuroscience data analysis.

🔍 Overview

  • NS‑Copilot is an LLM‑driven multi‑agent system for neuroscience analysis.
  • It autonomously supports end‑to‑end workflows for diverse professional tasks.
  • The system unifies domain‑specific pre‑trained models.
  • It supports key neuroscience modalities, including EEG and extracellular spike data, through a natural‑language interface.

🧩 How it works

  • Given raw data and a task description, NS‑Copilot orchestrates agents with specialized roles:
    • Planning
    • Adaptive control
    • Code generation
    • Result synthesis
  • This orchestration enables analysis without dataset‑specific heuristics.

Supported modalities

Modality Supported
EEG ✅
Extracellular spike data ✅

📊 Evaluation

  • NS‑Copilot was evaluated on neuroscience benchmarks spanning:
    • Alzheimer’s disease
    • Parkinson’s disease
    • Working memory spike decoding
  • Across 8 trials per task, the system consistently outperformed strong baselines on the primary metric.

💡 Why it matters

  • Demonstrates effective and scalable neuroscience analysis using LLM‑driven multi‑agent coordination.
  • Reduces the need for hand‑crafted, dataset‑specific heuristics.
  • Provides a natural‑language interface that can streamline complex analytical pipelines for researchers.

#Neuroscience #LLM #MultiAgent #AI #NS-Copilot

Source: NS-Copilot: An LLM-Driven Agent System for Autonomous Neuroscience Analysis
